output:
*Interview with Rosa Häfeli, cook and maid, in the dining room. Second interview of the night.*

MATTHEY: Good morning, Mademoiselle Häfeli. Thank you for waiting. Please sit down. You are not in trouble. I only want you to tell me, in your own way, how the evening went in the kitchen.

ROSA: Ja, I am sitting. Herrgott, I have been sitting since your men came up the stairs. I do not know what to do with my hands.

MATTHEY: Then rest them on the table. Tell me about the kitchen first.

ROSA: It is my kitchen. Monsieur did not like people in it, but Madame knows what I am worth. Everything was ready for the toast. I had washed the champagne glasses myself that afternoon and polished them twice, because Monsieur looks at glasses before he looks at the food. For the new century, the glasses were on the tray and the bread was cut.

MATTHEY: You keep a clock in the kitchen.

ROSA: The American one, on the shelf by the stove. It is a quarter of an hour fast. I keep it so on purpose, so nothing is ever late. The soup is never late, Madame's coffee is never late. Monsieur used to laugh at me. He said a cook who cheats her clock will cheat her master. I said I do not cheat, I only start early.

MATTHEY: You are sure of the quarter hour?

ROSA: I am sure. I set it myself, every Sunday, for ten years. A quarter and no more.

MATTHEY: Let us come to the evening, when you were downstairs. Tell me what you remember.

ROSA: Fräulein Lina came down into the kitchen at thirteen minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock, and she stayed with me until after the temple struck eleven. She was white. She had been working up in the atelier with the master, and then he sent her down, and she came to me to be near someone. She sat on the stool and did not say much. I gave her a cup of coffee and she did not drink it. She is a good girl, she does not complain. But her lips were moving, as if she were counting something, and when I asked she only shook her head.

MATTHEY: Go on, please.

ROSA: We heard Madame's piano begin at two minutes to eleven by my kitchen clock. Chopin. Madame plays the nocturnes when she is tired, or when she does not want to talk. Fräulein Lina and I sat and listened, and it was beautiful, Herrgott, it was beautiful, and the kitchen was warm. Then it stopped at eleven minutes past eleven by my kitchen clock. I looked at the clock then because I wanted to get on with the glasses.

MATTHEY: Did you hear the hall clock?

ROSA: The old Morbier in the hall, yes. I heard the hall clock strike eleven when my kitchen clock showed thirteen minutes past eleven. I did not think about it. I was thinking about the bread.

MATTHEY: And after that?

ROSA: After that I went up to fetch the master for the toast. Madame had sent me. I went up the back stairs to the atelier, and I called to him, and he did not answer. He was on the floor under the long windows. I will not tell you more than that, Monsieur, I cannot. The regulator on the wall had stopped, and his hand was closed on his watch. I thought, he is only fallen asleep, he will be cross that I woke him. Then I saw his face.

MATTHEY: You went for help?

ROSA: I went down. I did not run, I walked, because Madame was at the piano and I did not want to frighten her. I found her in the salon, and she looked at me, and she knew before I said a word. She is a strong woman, Madame. She stood up and said, "Rosa, fetch Dr Vauthier." That is what she said. Then she said, "No, fetch the police first," and I did not know which to do, so I did both.

MATTHEY: You are loyal to Madame.

ROSA: Loyal? I have been in this house twenty-two years. I would not leave her now, not for all the Morbier clocks in the canton.

MATTHEY: Do you fear the police, Mademoiselle?

ROSA: Ja. I am from the Emmental, we do not like men in uniform in our kitchens. I have done nothing wrong. But you are a Neuchâtel man with your questions, and I am only a cook, and I do not know what a cook is supposed to say to a sûreté inspector at this hour. So I say what I saw, and I say it slowly, and if I am wrong about a minute you must forgive me, because it is not my clock that is wrong. It is the one I keep for the house.

MATTHEY: Thank you, Mademoiselle. That is very clear.

ROSA: Then may I go back to my kitchen? The bread will not wait.
